fields.meaning: The same state continues without any change.
examples: to end up never meeting
I promised to meet him, but in the end we never did meet.
The laundry has been left hanging outside the whole time.

fields.connection: まるで + Nの / V plain form + よう(だ)
examples: I passed! It's just like a dream.
His Japanese sounds just as if a Japanese person were speaking.
I can't understand what you're saying at all.
fields.explain: Used when you want to compare a thing or action to a high degree, equivalent to something others could hardly imagine or believe.

fields.connection: Aい (drop い) + み / Na + み
examples: a rounded shape, white tinged with blue, a board with some thickness
The principal says the same thing at the entrance ceremony every year. There's nothing fresh about it at all.
"I'm looking forward to the day I can meet you."
fields.explain: Turns certain adjectives into nouns with ～み to express the degree, feeling or nuance of a quality. It cannot be used with every adjective.
fields.notes:
1) It is easy to misread ～み as "try doing" (～てみる).
→ Here ～み turns an adjective into a noun to talk about a "feeling/degree..."; it has nothing to do with ～てみる.
2) Not every adjective can take ～み.
→ Only certain fixed adjectives are commonly used (such as 痛み, 苦み...); do not make up your own forms in the exam.
3) Easily confused with ～さ.
→ ～さ is usually used to measure/quantify (height, length...); ～み leans toward perception/sensory quality.

fields.connection: V plain form + かも かもしれない かもしれません / N / Na / Aい
examples: His story might possibly be a lie.
I might not be able to go tomorrow.
fields.explain: Used to describe the speaker's conjecture, often based on intuition

fields.meaning: Giving a reason (often like "because...", common among women/children)
fields.connection: V plain form + ものだから ものですから もんだから (spoken) / N + な / Na / Aい
examples: "Why were you late?" "I'm sorry, the train stopped because of an accident."
Because I'm usually healthy, I was overconfident and ended up collapsing from overwork.
"My father is ill, you see, so I need money for all sorts of things."
"I didn't know you were a teacher, so I'm terribly sorry for being rude."
fields.explain: Used to give a subjective reason, as an explanation or excuse. 「もので」 is more polite than 「ものだから」.
fields.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～から／～ので.
→ ～ものだから／もので is an explanation that sounds like a justification or excuse; it is subjective.
2) Distinguishing ものだから and もので.
→ もので is usually more neutral/polite; ものだから leans toward spoken language.
3) Not used for objective, formal causes.
→ If the reason is "because of the rules / because of the figures," use ～ため／～ので.

fields.meaning: Spoken language expressing an excuse and a reason.
examples: because it's inconvenient
"You didn't come yesterday, did you?" "Sorry, something urgent came up."
My friend came over to hang out, so I ended up playing instead of studying.

fields.name: ～ようだ／～みたいだ（conjecture）
fields.meaning:
Expresses conjecture based on what one feels or sees.
［ふつう］　+　ようだ／みたいだ
［N：雨な／N：雨の　+　ようだ」
元気／N：雨　+　みたいだ］
fields.connection: V/A plain form + ようだ・みたいだ / Nの/Naな + ようだ / N/Na + みたいだ（conjecture）
examples: seems to be unwell
Mr. Tanaka seems to be unwell today.
The room next door is noisy. It looks like they're having a party.

fields.meaning: Tried to / was about to... but
fields.connection: V volitional form + とした(ら/ところ)（just as one was about to do..., ...）
examples: Just as I was about to leave the house, I got a call from my boss.
I tried to open the door, but the lock was broken and it wouldn't open.
I tried to tell him the truth, but I couldn't.
Just as I was about to get on the train, I realized I had forgotten my wallet.
The moment I was about to fall asleep, the room next door got noisy.
Just as I was about to go home, an urgent request came in.
fields.explain:
Used to describe an immediate intention at a past point in time, often together with an interrupting event or an unsuccessful result.
V-ようとしたら／ところ／途端(に): emphasizes surprise, right at the moment of the intended action.
V-ようとしたが／ものの: emphasizes effort that failed.
The form V-ようとしていた: provides the background of "was about to" lasting for a short while.
Not used for long-term plans; use ～つもりだった for plans.

• Meaning 1: "Was about to do ... when ..." — emphasizes the moment just before carrying out the action, with another event intervening.
• Meaning 2: "Tried to do ... (but did not succeed)" — connected with が／ものの to show a result contrary to expectation.
• Meaning 3: The nuance of being "on the verge" — the action almost happened but in the end did not take place or was prevented.
• Analysis: とした is the past of とする, describing an intention at a point in time that has passed; it is often followed by a second clause expressing an obstacle, a contrary result or an unexpected event.
• The subject is usually the speaker or an agent with volition; it is rarely used with inanimate subjects.
fields.notes:
• With verbs that do not express volition (rain, happen), avoid ～ようとした; use ～ところ／～直前など instead.
• Attaching としたら gives a stronger nuance of surprise than としたところ.
• In narrative writing, ～ようとした瞬間／矢先(に) often appears to build a climax.
mistakes: Using it with a non-volitional verb: ×雨が降ろうとした → 〇雨が降り出した／降りそうだった。
Confusing it with ～つもりだった: ～ようとした means "about to, right at that moment," not a plan made in advance.
Omitting the second clause: many sentences need a result/obstacle clause after ～とした to be complete.
Wrong tense: to say "is about to," use ～ようとしている, not ～ようとした.
JLPT: often tests the distinction between としたら (surprise) and としたが (result contrary to expectation).

rows: Was about to / tried (but did not succeed)
<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>かけようとしたが、<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>。
Not past; the action is ongoing
About to / in the middle of / just did
Three tenses: ところだ／ところに／ところで
Long-term intention, no emphasis on the moment
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>くつもりだったが、<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>けなかった。

examples: I like bright colors like red and pink.
I also want to be able to speak Japanese well like Lin soon.
"I want a sweater like the one you're wearing, too."
In a big country like America, it's only natural that there are time differences within the country.
fields.explain: Used to compare, give examples or express similarity: like..., similar to.... Often used when describing an image, a situation or a way of doing something.
fields.notes:
1) It is easy to confuse the functions of ～ような and ～ように.
→ ～ような comes before a noun; ～ように usually modifies a verb or a clause.
2) Easily confused with ～みたいだ.
→ ～ような／ように is neutral and can be used in written language; ～みたいだ leans toward spoken language.
3) Do not take it to mean "exactly the same."
→ This pattern usually indicates similarity or gives examples. | Also used to give typical examples (例示)

fields.name: ～ように（introductory remark・as is known）
fields.meaning:
…の内容がすでに知られていると前置きする
An introductory remark saying that the content of ... is already known.
examples: Like humans, plants also need nutrients.
Just as their mother was a cheerful person, her daughters also have cheerful personalities.
We're not in the kind of relationship you're imagining.
As I told you before, I won't be in Japan next week.
As it said in this morning's paper, the rice harvest seems to be good this year.
As you know, Japan is a country with many typhoons.
fields.notes:
It is also used when instructing others to do something ⏐ examples: 1. 皆様ご存じのように、試験の内容が変わります。
As you all know, the content of the exam will change
2. ここに書いてあるように、今度の木曜日、授業は午前中だけです。
As written here, this coming Thursday there will be classes only in the morning.
3. 前にお話ししたように、来年から授業料が値上がりします。
As I said before, tuition will go up from next year

examples: For your health, try to chew your food well when you eat.
Let's try not to make noise in the elevator.
Let's make sure to be on time for appointments.
To rest your eyes, try to stand up at least once an hour.
Let's try not to stay up late.
Let's make a point of greeting people in a loud, clear voice.
fields.explain:
Has a gentle, polite nuance; more of a guideline/instruction than a command.
Suitable for contexts such as: announcements at a company or school, information signs, speeches.
For an immediate action, "～ましょう/～てください" is more natural. For a long-term habit, use "～ようにしましょう".
The subject is usually an implied "みなさん/私たち" and does not need to be stated.

• The pattern "～ようにしましょう" expresses an appeal/advice to make a steady effort together or build a habit: "Let's try to .../let's be careful to ...".
• Unlike "～ましょう" (just an invitation to do something right now), "～ようにしましょう" focuses on maintaining/paying attention to a principle or repeated behavior.
• The negative form can be used to advise avoiding a behavior: "～ないようにしましょう".
• Often appears in public announcements, rules, health/safety recommendations, classrooms and instruction manuals.
fields.notes:
• The negative form "～ないようにしましょう" is very common in safety/work contexts: 転ばないようにしましょう。
• When the goal is "to become able to do," use the potential form: 毎日少しずつ読んで、新聞が読めるようにしましょう。
• In long-term guidance, add "～ていきましょう" to emphasize the process: 省エネを続けていくようにしましょう。
mistakes: Attaching it directly to a noun is wrong: ×健康ようにしましょう → ○健康に気をつけるようにしましょう。
Using it for an immediate action sounds awkward: ×ドアを閉めるようにしましょう（right now） → ○ドアを閉めましょう。
Confusing it with "～ようにする": the latter describes one's own habit, not an appeal to others.

rows: <ruby>遅<rt>おく</rt></ruby>れないようにしてください。
<ruby>早<rt>はや</rt></ruby>く<ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>るようにする。
A specific decision, no emphasis on habit
<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>は<ruby>休<rt>やす</rt></ruby>むことにしましょう。

fields.connection: Vる/V potential form + ようになった
examples: I practiced every day, and now I can play the piano.
As I've gotten older, I've started getting up early.
I no longer walk while looking at my smartphone.
The lights are designed to turn off automatically.
This town has gradually come to see more tourists.
After changing my glasses, I can now read even small print.
fields.explain:
More natural and objective than "～ようにする" (intentional action). Emphasizes the result of a change that has taken place.
Used to report growth, progress or a change of habit.
For natural phenomena/designs, use "～ようになっている" instead of "～ようになった".

• Expresses a "change of state" over time: from not doing → starting to do; from not being able → being able.
• Emphasizes the result achieved after a process, often due to circumstances/practice/outside influence.
• Negative form: "Vないようになった" = stopped/no longer does (change of habit).
• "～ようになっている" describes a mechanism/design that leads to a certain result.
fields.notes:
• Ability: 走れる/話せる/見られる + ようになった expresses "have become able to ..." after practice.
• With devices/procedures: ～ように（自動で）なる/なっている states the intended mechanism/design.
• Avoid attaching it directly to adjectives to say "became ...ようになった": use ～く/～に なってきた/なった. Example: ×暑いようになった → ○暑くなってきた。
mistakes: Confusing it with "～ようにする": that one is effort; "～ようになった" is the result of a change.
Using it for unconscious natural phenomena: prefer ～なくなった over ～ないようになった when there is no element of control.
Do not attach it directly to adjectives: ×きれいようになった → ○きれいになった。

rows: An effort; the state may not have changed yet
<ruby>毎日<rt>まいにち</rt></ruby><ruby>走<rt>はし</rt></ruby>るようにする。
<ruby>毎日<rt>まいにち</rt></ruby><ruby>走<rt>はし</rt></ruby>るようになった。
<ruby>転勤<rt>てんきん</rt></ruby>することになった。
Natural/degree, no emphasis on a goal
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>らなくなった。
Change of habit due to awareness/circumstances
<ruby>酒<rt>さけ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>飲<rt>の</rt></ruby>まないようになった。

fields.meaning:
Expresses what one perceives. Also used to state one's own opinion gently.
［ふつう］　+　ように　+　感じる／見える／思う
［Na：元気な　N：子供の］
fields.connection: V/A plain form + ように感じる
examples: I felt there couldn't be a better room than this.
I feel he has changed a little since graduating from college.
When I wear these clothes, I look fat.
I think this color might be better...

fields.name: ～ように（like／as）
fields.meaning: So that..., in order to... (achieve a state/purpose)
examples: It's normal for children not to turn out the way their parents want.
"Everyone, please move your body as I tell you from now on."
"As this book also says, water shortages are becoming a serious problem in many parts of the world."
"As I mentioned the other day, Mr. Sato is being transferred, so I'd like to hold a farewell party next week."
I left home at 8 so that I would make the 9 o'clock shinkansen.
My mother takes care of all sorts of things so that the family can live comfortably.
fields.explain:
Used to compare or to cite content: "like..., as...".
Expresses a purpose of achieving some result: "so that...".

Like / as ...
In order to achieve a purpose ...
fields.notes:
1) It is easy to confuse the many meanings of ～ように.
→ It has the meaning "like/as" and the meaning "so that (purpose)".
2) Look at the second clause to decide.
→ If the second clause is an action/instruction: it is usually the purpose meaning.
→ If it is a comparison/citation of content: it is the "like/as" meaning.
3) Easily confused with ～ために.
→ ～ように is often used when the purpose concerns an ability/result to be achieved; ～ために is usually more direct.

fields.connection: Vる → V passive form + た (噛まれた・褒められた)
examples: I was bitten on the hand by a dog.
I was praised by my teacher.
I was able to sleep soundly last night.
The company president came to the meeting. (keigo)
I got caught in a sudden rain shower.
The person next to me kept talking to me the whole time.
fields.explain:
Passive: neutral or with a nuance of disadvantage/annoyance depending on the context.
Past potential: only natural with Group 2 verbs and 来る（来られた）; Group 1 verbs use ～えた (書けた,行けた), not ～られた.
Passive keigo: formal, used for superiors/customers. Consider using special honorific forms:召し上がった, いらっしゃった.

• Past passive: The action has happened; the subject is the person/thing affected. Example: 先生に注意された。
• Past potential (Group 2/来る): Expresses "was able to ..." (could sleep, could see). Example: よく見られた（=見える/見られるの過去）.
• Passive keigo: Shows respect for the person doing the action. Example: 部長はもうお帰りになられた／帰られた。
• Adversative passive: Expresses annoyance caused by a behavior/phenomenon. Example: 隣で大声で歌われた。
fields.notes:
• The agent in the passive is usually marked with に; when emphasizing the means/cause, use によって/で: 風に吹かれた／台風によって家が壊された。
• "見られた" can mean "was seen" (passive) or "was able to see" (potential of 一段). Context is needed to tell them apart.
• The adversative passive can be used with natural phenomena: 雪に降られた, 風に吹かれた.
mistakes: Confusing the Group 1 potential: ×行られた → ○行けた.
Missing the agent marker に in the passive: ×先生を叱られた → ○先生に叱られた.
Confusing it with keigo: "来られた" can be keigo, not passive. Use the subject to tell them apart.
Using から to mark the agent: ×先生から褒められた → ○先生に褒められた（によって is also correct but more formal/academic）.

rows: <ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>叱<rt>しか</rt></ruby>られる。
Formal; avoids ambiguity with the passive
<ruby>社長<rt>しゃちょう</rt></ruby>はお<ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>りになった。
<ruby>残業<rt>ざんぎょう</rt></ruby>させられた。

fields.name: ～れる／られる（spontaneous）
fields.connection: Group 1: V (a-row) + れる / Group 2: Vます(drop ます) + られる / する → される / 来る → こられる
examples: Whenever I hear this song, I can't help remembering my childhood.
When I see the package sent from home, I find myself thinking of my mother.
I can't help worrying about my grandmother, who lives alone in the countryside.
I hear my younger sister's illness is hard to cure with modern medicine. Everyone is eagerly awaiting the completion of a new drug.
fields.explain: Expresses emotions, thoughts or actions that arise naturally, unintentionally.
fields.notes:
1) Easily confused with the ordinary passive (someone has something done to them by someone).
→ Here ～れる／られる expresses emotions/thoughts that arise naturally (spontaneously), with no emphasis on the agent.
2) Often used with verbs such as 思われる・思い出される.
→ It means "can't help feeling/remembering/worrying...".
3) Not used to describe a specific harm suffered.
→ If there is a clear agent (A does B), use the ordinary passive.

examples: He looks young for his age.
You did well for a first time.
For a cheap restaurant, this place gives small portions.
For someone who has lived in Japan for a long time, I can't read kanji.
Even though it's a quiet place, I can't concentrate.
fields.explain:
Place the "standard of comparison" before ～わりには, then give a result/evaluation contrary to expectation in the second clause.
Suitable for both spoken and written language; "であるわりには" is more formal.
Often carries a slight nuance of criticism/surprise; avoid putting a command/volitional expression (～しなさい、～ましょう) right after it.
The sense of contrast can be emphasized with a following connective: ～わりには、意外と／案外／思ったより…

- Expresses an evaluation that is "out of proportion/different from expectation" based on a stated standard. Translation: "considering...", "for...", "and yet".
- Nuance: normally standard A would be expected to lead to B, but in reality it is C (different, or lower/higher than expected). Often implies surprise, contrary to common sense.
- Mainly used in comments and evaluations. Not used with a direct command/volition right after ～わりには.
fields.notes:
• Nouns indicating age/experience very often go with ～のわりには: 年齢のわりには／初心者のわりには.
• In conversation, the second part can be omitted if the context is clear: この値段のわりには…（いいね）.
• With quantities: 量／価格／点数／頻度 のわりには…
explain: Expresses a result that differs from the normal degree or way of thinking: "considering..., ...".
examples: 1. 「山田さんは留学経験がないわりに英語の発音がきれいですね」
Yamada has never studied abroad, but his English is good.
2. この仕事は大変なわりに給料が安い。
This job is hard, and yet the pay is low.
3. あのレストランは値段のわりに（＝値段が安いわりに）おいしくて量も多い。
That restaurant is cheap, yet the food is good and the portions are large too.
4. 彼女はやせているわりには丈夫で力も強い。
She is thin but healthy.
5. ＊今度の試験はあまり勉強しなかった。そのわりには成績がまあまあでほっとした。
I didn't study much for this exam. Even so, my results were fairly good, which was a relief. meaning_vi: Even though, despite ⏐ explain: Used when describing or showing a case where a thing or event runs contrary to common sense or what is natural.
Expresses a feeling of surprise, something unexpected ⏐ examples: 1. 年のわりには若く見える。
Despite his age, he still looks young
2. お金がない（と言っている）わりに、よく買い物をするね。
You have no money, and yet you shop a lot
mistakes: Wrong "助詞": writing 子どもわりには × correct: 子どものわりには.
Confusing it with ～だけあって (meets expectations). The JLPT often sets traps by reversing the praise/criticism nuance.
Using it with a command: ～わりには、行きなさい × (avoid). Use a different structure.
Forgetting "な" with な-adjectives: 静かわりには × correct: 静かなわりには.

rows: Judging by standard A, B is surprising
Close in meaning; ～にしては is usually for a "clear, specific standard"
<ruby>子<rt>こ</rt></ruby>どもにしてはよく<ruby>頑張<rt>がんば</rt></ruby>った。
Compared with A, the result differs from expectation
The standard can be subjective or based on common sense; used widely
<ruby>値段<rt>ねだん</rt></ruby>のわりには<ruby>質<rt>しつ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>い。
<ruby>知<rt>し</rt></ruby>っているくせに<ruby>教<rt>おし</rt></ruby>えない。
Opposite nuance: the result matches expectations
<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>いだけあって<ruby>品質<rt>ひんしつ</rt></ruby>がいい。
